sm: The grand opening of the Merrill Williams Heritage and Cultural Center begins with welcome remarks from the master of ceremonies, who calls the day a profound milestone for the African American Heritage Society of Williamson County. Board members and public officials are recognized, and Reverend Boyce Wilkins gives an invocation giving thanks for the building as a place where history will be preserved and generations connected. Senator Jack Johnson's chief of staff, Luke Gustafson, says the senator is traveling to East Tennessee to survey flood damage with the House Speaker, and notes that Republican colleagues had just nominated him for Speaker of the Senate.

Luke Gustafson congratulates the society and presents a proclamation from Lieutenant Governor Randy McNally on behalf of Senator Johnson. Franklin Mayor Ken Moore then speaks, recalling that the city named A and C Williams Way to honor a merchant who ran a Main Street business after becoming a free man, and he remembers knocking on Fred Williams's door while campaigning in 2007. Williamson County Mayor Andy Marshall says he ran on faith, family and community, and begins reading a county proclamation. It honors the society's nearly four years of planning and preservation that turned the property at 264 Natchez Street into the center.

Mayor Marshall finishes the county proclamation recognizing the grand opening. Society president Alma McLemore and founding member Mary Pearce then thank the community and the donors. They single out Emily McGinn, whose lead gift made the project possible, and say a group of women raised over one hundred twenty thousand dollars for a room named in honor of a trailblazer. They also thank the Tennessee economic development grant secured with help from Senator Johnson. The emcee then introduces people involved from the start, including attorney Julian Beale, historian Dr. Carroll Van West, Lamont Turner, Jeffrey Carus and Kenneth Green, who covered monthly expenses.

Julian Beale recounts how, in December 2020, calls from the Battle of Franklin Trust, the Land Trust for Tennessee and Dr. Van West alerted him that the Natchez Street house was for sale. He emailed about thirty-five community leaders, and Cassandra Williams agreed to sell to a group with no money, giving them a year. Donors covered expenses, and the group raised the money in about seven months and closed on November 12, 2021, exactly four years earlier. He describes the site's history, from the federal line in 1864 to the Williams family home. Dr. Van West then speaks, clarifying that he is still Tennessee State Historian, and recalls first touring the house.

Dr. Van West says the society had developed over twenty or thirty years and deserved a headquarters to tell its own stories. He explains that he and Cassandra Williams chose which items to keep so real objects would tell the family's story. He says no one in the nation does history better than Franklin and urges support for the center. Lamont Turner then shares that his inspiration was a childhood memory of Mr. Fred Williams giving him and his grandmother taxi rides, recalling his white hair and the pencil behind his ear. He says preserving landmarks protects sacred memories and helps the next generation connect to the past.

Another donor speaks briefly, saying it was a labor of love. Mary Pearce then recognizes major donors, including Miss Emily's million dollar gift, Calvin and Marilyn, the Tennessee Department of Economic and Community Development, and several local organizations and churches. She says the budget began near eight hundred thousand dollars, and the project came to about two million dollars. A contractor thanks everyone, describing the challenges of a house over one hundred years old, built before modern standards and converted from residential to commercial use. Representatives of the Tennessee Historical Commission and the State Historic Preservation Office are then introduced, and one thanks the community for the grant funding and ongoing consultation.

The Tennessee Historical Commission speakers call the center a place to reflect on the lives of African Americans who shaped the community. The emcee then introduces Williamson County's African American historian, a founding member of the Heritage Society. She remembers the neighborhood as a segregated community and Fred Williams as a believer in history who mentored the society, with fish fries in the backyard. She introduces his daughter Cassandra Williams, describing her upbringing on Natchez Street, her great grandfather's shop on Main Street, her career in Memphis, and her family's lasting impact. She urges everyone to tell their story.

Cassandra Williams says the center will be called the Merrill Williams home but will always be remembered as the home of Mr. Fred and Miss Maddie. She introduces her children, her granddaughter and relatives, and recalls summers in Franklin, her mother's cooking and her father's garden, taxi rides and antique gun collection. She says she would love to move back but cannot afford it, and thanks every donor, calling the center a dream she never wants to wake up from. Her family then gathers on the porch, and the ribbon is cut as the center is declared open.
